name: Cacio e Pepe (Roman Cheese & Pepper Pasta)
why: The real Roman method for cacio e pepe — no cream, no butter, just pecorino, black pepper and starchy pasta water emulsified into a glossy sauce. The 'spread the cheese paste around the bowl' trick is a genuinely satisfying technique, and it's a 20-minute midweek supper that's hard to beat in winter.
author: Henry
ingredients: 200g spaghetti (or tonnarelli, if you can find it)

steps: Bring a saucepan of well-salted water to a rolling boil.
Meanwhile, in a large bowl combine the pecorino and black pepper. Gradually incorporate 2–3 tablespoons of hot pasta water (once you have some) to make a thick paste.
Using the back of a dessertspoon, spread the cheese paste evenly up the sides of the bowl — this is the key move.
Cook the spaghetti in the boiling water according to the packet instructions, to al dente.
About halfway through cooking, scoop out a mugful of the starchy cooking water and set aside.
Drain the pasta and leave it to rest in the pan for 1 minute — this stops it steaming so the cheese doesn't seize.
Tip the hot pasta into the bowl with the cheese paste. Working quickly off the heat, toss and swirl the strands so the residual heat melts the cheese and coats the pasta.
Add little drizzles of the starchy cooking water as you go until you have a glossy, flowing sauce that clings to the strands.
Serve immediately, straight from the bowl, with a final grating of pecorino and crack of black pepper.

pro_tips: Grate the pecorino with a microplane rather than a coarse grater — fine grating melts into the emulsion; coarse shreds don't.
Keep everything off direct heat: the pasta's own residual heat is what melts the cheese. If the cheese seizes into clumps, it's too hot — add a splash more pasta water and keep tossing.
